newsitem.title: USA: U.S. consumer stocks rally amid earning worries.
newsitem.headline: U.S. consumer stocks rally amid earning worries.

text.p: Investors, spooked by signs of a slowing U.S. economy, on Thursday bought shares in consumer products companies seen more likely to produce steady earnings in a slowdown.

With the third-quarter earnings reporting period approaching, so-called defensive stocks, including those in drug, beverage and food companies, jumped on Thursday. Stocks in companies whose profits are seen more vulnerable to swings in economic activity trailed.
The catalyst for the move was a report of a sharp 3.1 percent drop in new orders for durable goods in August.
"I think they're worried about the economy," Jack Regan, Josepthal, Lyon and Ross analyst, said of investors' mood.

Drug makers were up across the board, with Merck and Co Inc gaining 1-7/8 to 70-3/4, Warner-Lambert Co rising 2-5/8 to 66-3/8, Eli Lilly and Co gaining 1-7/8 to 64-7/8 and Amgen Inc up 1-3/8 to 64-3/4.
Among others, Coca-Cola Co rose 3/4 to 52, Procter & Gamble Co added 3/4 to 96-5/8 and ConAgra Inc gained 1-1/8 to 48-1/8.

Analysts expect the Standard & Poor's 500 year-over-year operating earnings to rise by 6.1 percent in the quarter that ends September 30, according to First Call. The group's earnings rose 10.1 percent in the second quarter.
Hugh Johnson, Chief Investment Officer at First Albany, said consumer non-cyclical stocks have been outperforming cyclical stocks for the past three weeks, only gaining steam on Thursday.
This could be a sign of a broadening concern on Wall Street over corporate profits beyond the third quarter and going into 1997, he said.
The durable goods data "supports the view that 1997 is going to be a tough year for profits," Johnson said.
Another driver of the move toward consumer stocks has been third quarter profit warnings, which have come from companies including Motorola Inc, AT&T, Silicon Graphics and Walbro Corp.
"I worry about the third quarter earnings because they're going to tell us about 1997," Johnson said.

But some companies, including Intel Corp and DuPont have announced expectations of stronger-than-expected third quarter, while 3Com Corp on Tuesday reported quarterly profits above Wall Street forecasts.
"I think it's going to be a mixed bag," Regan said of third quarter results.
Export demand, inventory restocking and strong consumer confidence indicates the U.S. economy "is not rolling over and playing dead," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal.
"On balance the earnings picture still is very vibrant, certainly for the third quarter just ended," he said. "The fourth quarter is also quite good."
A key factor in gauging 1997's economic outlook, and the stock market's reaction to it, will be the outcome of November's presidential and congressional elections, Battipaglia said.
